a9de8e575d9f40cd: SHAH ALAM: The defence team representing the 15-year-old boy acquitted of murdering his schoolmate last year is ready to face the prosecution's appeal against the decision.
Lawyer Kitson Foong said the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) appeal was expected given the gravity of the case and the grief suffered by the victim's family.
"An appeal by the A-GC in a matter of this magnitude and tragic public resonance is, frankly, something any seasoned lawyer anticipates.

"Given the immense grief of the family and the overwhelming public emotion surrounding the case, it is entirely understandable, and perhaps inevitable that the prosecution seeks the appellate court's scrutiny.
"We are not surprised by the filing, nor are we unprepared," he said.
Foong said the defence would vigorously defend the Shah Alam High Court's findings, which were set out in a 77-page grounds of judgment.

"The learned trial judge delivered an exhaustive, exceptionally thorough 77-page grounds of judgment that meticulously examined months of unchallenged forensic psychiatric evidence, statutory constraints, and complex legal precedents," he said.
He added that his team was fully prepared to argue the factual and legal findings before the appellate court.

"Our team is fully re-engaged and we look forward to ventilating and defending both the factual and legal findings of the High Court before the appellate bench with the utmost rigor and professional respect," he said.
On Sept 14, judge Adlin Abdul Majid acquitted and discharged the boy after finding him to have been of unsound mind at the time of the incident.
She ordered him to be detained and treated at Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta in Perak at the pleasure of the Sultan of Selangor.
The prosecution has filed a notice of appeal at the Court of Appeal.

The boy had pleaded not guilty to murdering his Form Four schoolmate under Section 302 of the Penal Code in the girls' toilet of SMK Bandar Utama Damansara (4), Bandar Utama, Petaling Jaya, between 9.20am and 9.35am on Oct 14 last year.
The charge carries the death penalty, or jail of between 30 and 40 years and 12 strokes of the rotan upon conviction.
However, under Section 97(1) of the Child Act, the death penalty cannot be imposed on a child who was below 18 when the offence was committed.

Instead, Section 97(2) provides for a convicted child to be detained at the pleasure of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong if the offence occurred in the Federal Territories, or the Ruler or Yang di-Pertua Negeri if it occurred in a state.
Adlin accepted Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta director and consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Ian Lloyd Anthony's largely unchallenged findings on the boy's mental condition.

"Based on the evidence set out in the psychiatric report, Dr Ian Lloyd diagnosed the boy with schizophrenia, of very early onset (before the age of 13) with psychopathic and sadistic traits," the grounds stated.
Adlin said the finding that the boy was not criminally responsible for the girl's death due to unsoundness of mind should not be interpreted as diminishing her life or her family's grief.

She said the case exposed how serious mental illness could progress in a child while remaining invisible to those around him, with potentially devastating consequences if warning signs were not recognised.

Adlin said if any good could emerge from the tragedy, there should be greater understanding among parents, schools, courts and the public of the warning signs and consequences of untreated mental illness in children.

e2ed1ea81a4ef8e2: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — The remains of the late Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali will be laid to rest beside the tomb of Tun Endon Mahmood, the late wife of Malaysia's fifth prime minister Tun Abdullah Ahmad Badawi.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil disclosed this while sharing the funeral arrangements, after paying his respects at Dr Hasmah's family residence in Seri Kembangan earlier this afternoon.
Her remains were brought to the As-Syarif Mosque in Seri Kembangan for funeral prayers, before being transported to the National Mausoleum in Putrajaya for burial later this evening.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi shared that his wife, Datin Seri Hamidah Khamis, had met with Dr Hasmah just last week through their shared ties in the Welfare Association of Wives of Ministers and Deputy Ministers (Bakti).
Zahid said that Dr Hasmah's final conversation with his wife turned deeply spiritual, centring on faith and the afterlife.
“My wife told me that she (Dr Siti Hasmah) spoke a lot about God.
“She spoke a lot about the hereafter. She spoke a lot about the Assembly Place (Padang Mahsyar), as if she already knew that she would be leaving forever," Zahid said.
Dr Hasmah died this morning at the National Heart Institute (IJN) in Kuala Lumpur. She was 100.
ea55343def3c32e0: IPOH: Kementerian Kesihatan (KKM) hari ini melancarkan dua inisiatif pencegahan tingkah laku bunuh diri, iaitu National Suicide and Fatal Injury Registry Malaysia (NSFIRM) dan Garis Panduan Perkhidmatan Postvention.
Menteri Kesihatan Dzulkefly Ahmad berkata, NSFIRM ialah sistem registri yang akan memperkukuh pengumpulan data forensik kematian akibat bunuh diri dan kematian yang disebabkan oleh kecederaan.
“Pengumpulan data ini akan memudahkan analisis dan pemantauan trend kejadian secara lebih sistematik," katanya.
"Data yang tepat boleh digunakan bagi merancang polisi, program dan perkhidmatan yang lebih bersasar mengikut keperluan sebenar di lapangan."

Beliau berkata demikian dalam ucapan ketika menyempurnakan perasmian Hari Pencegahan Bunuh Diri Sedunia Peringkat Kebangsaan 2026 dan pelancaran dua inisiatif berkenaan di Dewan Utama Kolej Poly-Tech Mara hari ini.

Dzulkefly berkata, Garis Panduan Perkhidmatan Postvention pula memastikan individu yang terkesan susulan kejadian kematian bunuh diri mendapat sokongan psikososial dan intervensi bersesuaian bagi membantu proses pemulihan, di samping mengurangkan risiko berlakunya tingkah laku bunuh diri berulang (copycat suicide)

Dengan garis panduan ini, beliau berkata, perkhidmatan postvention dapat dilaksanakan dengan lebih tersusun, sistematik dan bersepadu, iaitu menerusi Pasukan Perkhidmatan Sokongan Kesihatan Mental dan Psikososial (MHPSS) yang memberikan sokongan kepada agensi dan komuniti yang terkesan.

Di samping itu, Dzulkefly berkata, KKM turut melaksanakan latihan dan pembangunan kapasiti bagi memperkukuh keupayaan agensi berkaitan, termasuk bersama Kementerian Pendidikan (KPM), Jabatan Kebajikan Masyarakat, NGO dan pihak berkepentingan yang lain.
Sementara itu, beliau berkata di Malaysia, data polis menunjukkan kes meningkat daripada 981 kes pada 2022 kepada 1,087 pada 2023 dan 1,114 pada 2024.
“Pada 2025, terdapat sedikit penurunan, iaitu 1,079 kes yang direkodkan, namun jumlah ini masih tinggi," tambahnya.

"Justeru, dengan tema ‘Ubah Tanggapan, Bina Harapan’ pada tahun ini, usaha pencegahan tingkah laku bunuh diri memerlukan komitmen daripada semua pihak dengan pendekatan keseluruhan kerajaan dan keseluruhan masyarakat.
“Dalam era digital ini, kami mempunyai tanggungjawab untuk memastikan maklumat yang dikongsi dan disebarkan tidak mendatangkan mudarat,” katanya.
Dalam pada itu, Dzulkefly menasihati orang ramai agar tindak merakam, menyebarkan atau menularkan kandungan berkaitan tingkah laku bunuh diri yang memaparkan kejadian secara sensasi.

Setiap daripada kita, katanya, mempunyai peranan sebagai masyarakat yang prihatin, lebih peka terhadap tanda-tanda awal masalah kesihatan mental dan lebih bersedia untuk menghulurkan bantuan kepada mereka yang sedang berdepan dengan krisis.
6cf9308b2752a3f2: PUTRAJAYA: A business partnership that went sour over more than RM2.4 million has ended with the Federal Court ruling that a joint venture partner can directly sue its former business partners to recover money it claimed had been misused or diverted.
The apex court allowed Pelorus Holding Sdn Bhd’s appeal against Jaffa Roger Dawkins, Rabiatul Adawiyyah Mohamad, and Harris Luqman Group Sdn Bhd.

Chief Justice Wan Ahmad Farid Wan Salleh, who sat with Federal Court judges Collin Lawrence Sequerah and Azimah Omar, said Pelorus was enforcing contractual obligations owed directly to it under the joint venture agreement (JVA).
He said the joint venture company, Pelorus HLG Sdn Bhd, had deliberately not been made a party to the JVA, even though it had already been incorporated when the agreement was signed.
“This was not a drafting oversight,” Wan Ahmad Farid said, adding that the parties had consciously chosen to bind themselves personally under the agreement.
Pelorus had provided funds for a joint venture involving livestock supply, integrated farming, breeding, abattoir operations, and meat products.
The relationship later broke down and Pelorus sued to recover money it claimed was owed to it.
Among its claims were RM1.19 million, which it said had been diverted for the benefit of Harris Luqman Group, and another RM1.21 million advanced to settle the joint venture company’s Agrobank loan.

The Court of Appeal had earlier ruled that the money belonged to the joint venture company and that any claim should therefore be brought by the company itself or through a derivative action, but the Federal Court disagreed.
Wan Ahmad Farid said Pelorus was not simply a shareholder complaining that the joint venture company had suffered a loss.
“The plaintiff is not an aggrieved shareholder complaining of a wrong done to its company, but is a contracting party claiming its due under a binding JVA,” he said.
He said Pelorus was seeking the return of its own money and enforcing obligations that the defendants had undertaken directly to it under the JVA.

The court also rejected an argument that Pelorus's funding arrangements amounted to illegal moneylending, finding that the advances were made as part of its contractual obligations under the joint venture.
However, the Federal Court dismissed Pelorus's separate claim for RM516,972, agreeing that the sum had not been properly substantiated.
Its RM1 million claim based on personal guarantees given by Dawkins and Rabiatul was allowed.
The defendants were also ordered to pay RM100,000 in costs.

David Mathews, S Shaarvin Raaj, K Ravvenneah and Reuben Choong appeared for Pelorus, while Hasshahari Johari Mawi, Rosly Khady Ayub Khan, Shah Nurul Afzan Abdullah and Nur Amni Irdina Mat Ayob acted for the respondents.
7fee98a0b714d458: SINGAPORE: A 37-year-old Malaysian was arrested at Tuas Checkpoint for allegedly attempting to smuggle drugs into Singapore, while a Singaporean was detained in a separate operation the same day, with the combined haul valued at over S$1 million (RM3.20 million).

The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) said the Malaysian was arrested on Sept 23 after officers found sealed packets labelled as commercial biscuits in the rear box of his Malaysia-registered motorcycle.
ICA said Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) officers were immediately alerted, and further checks uncovered more sealed packets.
"A total of about 6,961g of heroin, 1,116g of Ice and 1,032g of cannabis were seized from the motorcycle," ICA said in a statement.
Later that day, CNB officers launched an operation near Tampines Street 83, leading to the arrest of a 41-year-old Singaporean for suspected drug offences.
Officers seized 790g of heroin, 602g of cannabis, 127g of Ice, 51g of ecstasy tablets, 21g of ketamine, and S$33,086 in cash during the raid.
ICA said investigations are ongoing under Section 5 and Section 7 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973, which carries the death penalty for drug trafficking into Singapore.
"ICA will continue to work with CNB to prevent attempts to smuggle drugs across our borders," it added.
bbc95a3eb55917d2: SEPTEMBER 28 — Malaysia has lost more than the wife of a former prime minister. In the passing of Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali at the age of 100, the country has lost a remarkable Malaysian whose life traversed almost the entire history of modern Malaysia.

Her death at the National Heart Institute on September 28 was confirmed by her family. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim paid tribute to her lifelong contributions and service to Malaysia, while the King and Queen expressed their condolences to her family.

There will inevitably be different political views about her husband, Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad. That is the nature of democracy. Malaysia has lived through intense political contestation, particularly over the last decade.
But this is precisely the moment when Malaysians should know how to distinguish politics from humanity.
Dr Siti Hasmah deserves to be remembered in her own right.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali delivers a speech during the launch of Culture House at Menara Kuala Lumpur in this file photo taken on April 31, 2019. — Picture by Choo Choy May
Indeed, long before she became known internationally as the wife of Malaysia’s longest-serving prime minister, she had already broken barriers that younger Malaysians may find difficult to imagine.
Born in Klang in 1926, she entered the King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore after the Second World War on a scholarship.
She was the only Malay woman in her medical cohort. She graduated as a doctor in 1955 before beginning her housemanship at Kuala Lumpur General Hospital.
Consider what this meant in the social conditions of the time.
This was before Merdeka.
Opportunities for women in higher education were limited. Opportunities for Malay women to enter medicine were even rarer.
Dr Siti Hasmah nevertheless entered the profession and proceeded to build a career around one of the most fundamental dimensions of human security: the health of mothers and children.

In 1965, she became the first woman appointed as a Medical Officer in the Maternal and Child Health Department in Kedah. In 1974, she became the first woman to serve as the state’s Maternal and Child Health Officer.
Her work involved health programmes reaching rural communities at a time when access to modern healthcare could not be taken for granted.
This is the Dr Siti Hasmah Malaysians should remember.
Not merely the woman standing beside a powerful political leader, but the doctor standing beside mothers, children and families.
Her generation understood nation-building differently.
Malaysia was not constructed only in Parliament, government ministries or corporate boardrooms. It was built in schools, hospitals, rural clinics and communities.
Nation-building required people willing to serve quietly. Dr Siti Hasmah represented that tradition.
Her subsequent public life reflected the same concerns.

She was involved in organisations addressing family planning, maternal health, children’s rehabilitation, literacy, drug abuse and women’s welfare. Internationally, she participated in initiatives concerning rural women, mental health and drug abuse.
Yet what made her unusual was that her public presence rarely seemed dependent upon political power. She could be dignified without being distant.
She could be accomplished without constantly reminding Malaysians of her accomplishments.
And she could occupy the highest circles of Malaysian public life while retaining the warmth, humour and accessibility that became associated with her personality.

There was also another side to her that Malaysians came to appreciate: her love of music. She played the violin and piano, and even later in life remained curious enough to learn new things, including French and the erhu.
These may appear to be small details compared with the great political events through which she lived. They are not.
They tell us something important about ageing, learning and humanity. A meaningful life need not become narrower with age.
Curiosity can remain alive. Music can coexist with medicine. Public duty can coexist with humour.

Having reached her centenary only in July, Dr Siti Hasmah represented a living bridge across extraordinary periods of Malaysian history — colonialism, the Second World War, Merdeka, rapid development, industrialisation, political upheavals and the emergence of Malaysia as a significant middle power in Southeast Asia.
Few Malaysians have personally witnessed such an enormous arc of national transformation.
Her marriage to Tun Dr Mahathir, beginning in 1956, similarly stretched across seven decades of Malaysian history.
Yet Malaysians should resist turning this moment into another argument about Mahathirism, its achievements or its controversies.
There will be other days for those debates.
Today should be about Dr Siti Hasmah.
A mature nation must be capable of recognising humanity beyond political disagreement.
One can disagree profoundly with Tun Dr Mahathir’s politics and still acknowledge the extraordinary devotion of the woman who shared his life for seven decades.
One can belong to the government or opposition, or to no political party whatsoever, and still recognise what Dr Siti Hasmah represented.
Indeed, national unity does not require Malaysians to agree on everything.
It requires Malaysians to know when disagreement should yield temporarily to compassion.
There is something deeply Malaysian about mourning together.
Our society is composed of different races, religions, languages, regions and political traditions.
Yet death reminds us of something politics frequently causes us to forget: before we are partisans, we are human beings.
Dr Siti Hasmah’s life offers Malaysia an opportunity to rediscover that elementary truth.
Her century was remarkable not simply because she lived for 100 years.
It was remarkable because she used those years well.
She healed.
She served. She raised a family. She advocated for women and children. She represented Malaysia internationally. She played music.
She retained her humour. And throughout decades spent close to enormous political power, she preserved an identity recognisably her own.
That may ultimately be her greatest lesson.
Public life does not always have to be loud to be consequential.
Leadership does not always require a podium.
Service does not always seek recognition.
Sometimes the most enduring influence comes from dignity maintained consistently across a lifetime.
Malaysia therefore mourns not merely a former prime minister’s wife.

Malaysia mourns one of its pioneering women doctors, a public-health advocate, a mother, a musician, a witness to a century of national history and, above all, a Malaysian who demonstrated that grace and service can themselves constitute a form of leadership.
Whatever our politics, Malaysians can surely unite around that.
Rest in peace, Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali.
A remarkable Malaysian life has ended.
Its inspiration should not. Al Fatihah.
* Phar Kim Beng, PhD is the Professor of Asean Studies at International Islamic University of Malaysia and Director of Institute of International and Asean Studies (IINTAS).

64d3ab6e94b48b3d: SERI KEMBANGAN: Semua stesen radio dan televisyen diarahkan menukar rancangan serta program sepanjang hari ini sebagai tanda penghormatan kepada Dr Hasmah Ali.

a07a5d09a3de6626: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — Tabung Haji (TH) will open appeals for the 1448H/2027 Haj season via the THiJARI application and website from Oct 2, a month earlier than in the previous season.

TH Group managing director and chief executive officer Mustakim Mohamad said the earlier opening would give prospective pilgrims more time to prepare financially, physically and in terms of their knowledge of the Haj.

“The Haj payment for pilgrims selected through the appeal process is the full Haj cost of RM33,300 for the 1448H/2027 season, in line with the concept of istito’ah in fulfilling the obligation to perform the Haj.
“Applications are open to depositors who have at least RM15,000 in their respective TH accounts,” he said in a statement today.

Mustakim said TH had also introduced initiatives such as the #menujuistitoah campaign and the Seruan Istito’ah plan to help depositors prepare for the pilgrimage in a structured manner from an early stage.

Appeals to perform the Haj ahead of a depositor’s scheduled turn will be assessed based on merit criteria and scores, including the length of registration, age, average TH account balance, consistency of recurring savings, frequency of previous appeals and attendance at TH’s Basic Haj Course.
According to the statement, TH will also give priority to appeals involving mahram, companions of selected elderly pilgrims, and companions of selected persons with disabilities (PwD).
“The Haj payment for successful mahram or companion appeals will be based on the rate applicable to the selected pilgrim they are accompanying, according to the B40, M40 or T20 income group.
Meanwhile, prospective pilgrims are also reminded to make the necessary health preparations as approval of their applications is subject to medical screening.

Prospective pilgrims are also advised to equip themselves with sufficient knowledge of Haj rituals by attending TH’s Basic Haj Course, which will be conducted at more than 200 mosques nationwide from Sept 25.
Information, applications and the status of Haj appeals can be accessed through the THiJARI app or website at www.thijari.com.my.
For further information, the public may visit the Tabung Haji website or contact the Tabung Haji Contact Centre at 03-6207 1919. — Bernama
36dfd8c99ae533f4: KUALA LUMPUR: The existing parliamentary oversight bodies such as the rights and privileges committee are failing to deter abusive lawmakers because of slow procedures and weak reprimands, says former MP Kasthuri Patto.
The former Batu Kawan MP said the rights and privileges committee sits infrequently and allows offending MPs to avoid meaningful accountability with simple, insincere retractions.

“Sending an MP to the rights and privileges committee is a very light tap on the wrist because the committee doesn't sit very often," she said at a forum, titled “Women's Rights, Roles of MPs, and Government Obligations” here today.

“If the speaker doesn't call for a meeting or the MPs are unable to attend, the perpetrator is let off the hook. Or you see the next day that the perpetrator has said, ‘I’m sorry and I retract my comment’, only to do it again.”
Kasthuri said female and younger MPs regularly confront systemic gender bias and microaggressions by parliamentary staff and male MPs, who routinely assume lawmakers must be older men.
She shared instances of being mistaken for an administrative staff or targeted with personal insults in Parliament.
She said she did not take to heart insults such as “pendek” – “because I'm not that tall” – but felt it was inappropriate to ridicule or downplay an MP tasked with speaking for her constituents.
“We (the MPs) are among the 222 people bestowed with the right to speak for the 34 million Malaysians, and you look at me like I'm short?” she asked.
1caaf14cef504905: KAMPAR, Sept 28 — An elderly woman was found dead, believed to have been stabbed by her 49-year-old daughter in an incident at Lorong Kledang Utara 6, Taman Wang, Menglembu near Ipoh yesterday.

Perak police chief Datuk Mohd Alwi Zainal Abidin said the 70-year-old victim was found with a stab wound to her chest and was believed to have been killed by her daughter, who has a history of mental health treatment.
He said police received a report from the victim’s son-in-law at about 7pm.

“Her mother, who was bedridden and required intensive care, had just been brought home from an old folks’ home in Pusing and was being cared for by her daughter and son-in-law. The daughter also has a history of psychiatric treatment.

“We have detained the suspect, who will be remanded until Oct 4 to assist investigations under Section 302 of the Penal Code,” he told a press conference at the Kampar district police headquarters here today.
Mohd Alwi said police also seized a knife believed to have been used in the incident.

In a separate development, Mohd Alwi said the son of a disabled woman who was found dead at her home in Kampung Cheh Kati, Kuala Kangsar on Sept 23 had been sent to Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta for further treatment.
He said the 15-year-old boy had previously been remanded together with his 44-year-old father to assist investigations into the case.
The media previously reported that a 49-year-old woman was found dead, lying in a pool of blood in the living room of her house in the village.
Kuala Kangsar police chief ACP Heisham Harun said police received a report on the incident at 2.38pm after family members found the victim lying face down and unconscious. — Bernama

8ca647df8ad528d6: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — The proposed Freedom of Information Bill 2026 must genuinely provide access to information and should not impose excessive restrictions that undermine the purpose of the legislation, said Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said.
She said this was important to ensure the legislation achieved its intended objective, while taking into account the role and freedom of the media as part of the country’s democratic practices.

“You must make sure that if you have the FOI (Freedom of Information Act), it must be for information. You cannot have a bill where everything is prohibited from the outset... and I am very concerned about the media.

“For me, part of democracy in a country is to have that freedom of the media and have the full ability to do their work,” she told a press conference after the National Town Hall Public Hearing Session of the Special Select Committee (JKPK) on the Freedom of Information Bill 2026 at Parliament here today.

Azalina said the feedback received during the session showed positive responses to the proposed legislation, although the public wanted to see greater openness, with a balance still needing to be maintained.
She said the session also enabled the JKPK to hear views from the public, including the younger generation, while helping the committee review weaknesses identified in the existing blue bill.

“We need to look at it again because the blue bill that we have has many weaknesses. We see the weaknesses. So it’s good for this town hall and the public will know that the select committee members are extremely aware of the weaknesses and also understand that there is a need to have a balance,” she said.
On the next steps, Azalina said the JKPK would reconvene after the town hall session and review the issues raised before finalising the process.

“So far, this is only the national town hall. So we will come back for a select committee meeting soon and then we will relook. Basically, technically, there is the government bill, the blue bill and technically the select committee will also have their bill after this. So there will be like two bills,” she said.

Earlier, Azalina said in her welcoming remarks that the Freedom of Information Bill 2026 was tabled for its first reading in the Dewan Rakyat on July 13 before being referred to the JKPK on July 14, with several meetings and proceedings held since then to obtain the views of stakeholders.
She said the review must ensure that the legislation being introduced not only has good intentions but also clear provisions and implementation mechanisms.
“Good laws are not just laws that have good intentions. Good laws must have clear provisions and have application mechanisms that are understandable and can be implemented,” she said.

In July, Azalina said when tabling the Freedom of Information Bill 2026 for its first reading that the Bill was among the key measures to strengthen transparency, accountability and good governance, while enhancing public access to official government information in an orderly manner and in accordance with the law.
She said the Government also took note of various views raised by civil society organisations (CSOs) and stakeholders on several aspects of the Bill. — Bernama
f2ff856a6dcebf5f: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — The Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) has issued a thunderstorm warning for parts of Pahang, Sarawak, and Sabah, with heavy rain, gusty winds, and lightning expected to persist until 5pm today.
In Peninsular Malaysia, adverse weather conditions are forecast across three districts in Pahang, namely Cameron Highlands, Raub, and Bentong.
In Sarawak, the alert covers the Bintulu division (Bintulu and Sebauh), Miri, and the Limbang division.

In Sabah, the warning covers a wider area, encompassing Tawau, the Sandakan division (Tongod, Telupid, Kinabatangan, and Sandakan), the Interior division (Sook, Keningau, Tambunan, Membakut, and Pensiangan), alongside the West Coast division and Kudat.

MetMalaysia explained that a thunderstorm warning is triggered when atmospheric indicators point to impending storms with rainfall intensity exceeding 20mm per hour, or when precipitation is expected to last for more than an hour.
These alerts serve as short-term advisories and remain valid for a maximum duration of six hours from the time of issuance.

Residents in the affected areas are advised to stay vigilant, avoid open fields, steer clear of large trees and unstable structures, and prepare for potential flash floods, especially in low-lying zones and near slopes. Motorists have been urged to exercise extra caution on the road due to reduced visibility and slippery surfaces during heavy downpours.

259a1f8f6233a1cb: IPOH: A religious teacher at a national secondary school was charged at the sessions court here today with three counts of physical sexual assault against a 16-year-old male student two years ago.
Haslina Abu Bakar, 48, pleaded not guilty to the charges, read before judge Ainul Sharin Mohamad.
According to the first charge, Haslina is alleged to have committed physical sexual assault by kissing the boy on the mouth for sexual purposes in November 2024.
On the second charge, she is alleged to have committed the same act by hugging the victim a month later.
On the third charge, she is alleged to have committed physical sexual assault by having the victim touch her chest in November that same year.
The mother of six is alleged to have committed the acts in the Islamic education room of a national secondary school in Kinta.
The charges were framed under Sections 14(a) and 14(b) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017, which carries a maximum jail term of 20 years and caning upon conviction.

Deputy public prosecutor Nor Arfahanim Azureen Arfanuddin offered no bail on grounds that the offences were non-bailable, and taking into account the seriousness of the case as the accused was the victim's teacher. Nor Arfahanim also said that the student no longer attends the same school.
Haslina's lawyer, Amira Sofea An-Nur Ahmad, sought minimum bail, saying her client has six children between eight and 22 years of age who are still in school and higher learning institutions.
She said Haslina also suffers from high cholesterol and migraines, her husband has health problems, and she is the family's main source of income.

Amira Sofea also informed the court that Haslina is now serving at another school far from the victim, has a good service record as a teacher, is in permanent employment, and has no prior convictions.
The court allowed Haslina bail of RM10,000 with one surety and fixed Oct 28 for mention and the submission of documents.

Beliau berkata bagaimanapun sebarang perkembangan mengenai perkara itu, termasuk kemungkinan kenaikan gaji minimum kepada RM2,000, wajar menunggu pengumuman Perdana Menteri Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim mengenai Belanjawan 2027.

Beliau berkata bagi Kluang, sebanyak RM3.7 juta diperuntukkan termasuk bagi penambahbaikan 10 blok kuarters serta kerja pembaikan premis polis yang berada dalam pentadbiran IPD Kluang.
“Pendekatan ini memastikan peruntukan pembangunan disasarkan kepada keperluan sebenar dan memberikan impak kepada penyampaian perkhidmatan awam,” katanya.
d0df209185c601ed: SEPTEMBER 28 — For almost eight decades, Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad and Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali shared a marriage that became inseparable from the story of modern Malaysia.
Their marriage was exceptional — an extraordinary partnership that endured the demands of public life, the weight of power, its loss and the passage of time.
She supported him, cared for him and stood beside him, yet remained unmistakably herself, never disappearing into his shadow.

Siti Hasmah carried her grace and dignity like a crown — quietly, naturally, without ever needing to announce it. Whether Mahathir was Prime Minister or no longer in office, at the height of political power or standing outside it, she remained unmistakably herself.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali is seen at Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad’s meet and greet with the public at the Perdana Leadership Foundation, Putrajaya, in celebration of his 100th birthday July 10, 2025. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
She did not borrow her stature from him. She brought her own.

They met as young medical students, long before power, politics and public life entered their story. They were two doctors beginning their lives together, with no way of knowing where that journey would take them.

They would become husband and wife, parents, doctors, Prime Minister and Prime Minister’s wife. They would experience the demands of public life, the burden of power, its loss, and the remarkable return to politics of a 92-year-old husband whom she would once again follow into the fray.
But what made their marriage remarkable was what held it together: trust, companionship and the quiet instinct to look after one another.
It is a beautiful love story.
The deepest measure of that relationship was found not in the grand occasions, but in the smallest moments.
At Bersih 4 in 2015, when Mahathir decided to go into the crowd, Siti Hasmah would not let him go alone.
“I decided to be by his side to protect him,” she later wrote.
There was pushing and jostling as they entered the crowd. People wanted to shake their hands. The media surrounded them. Yet she stayed beside him.

The following day, they took the Komuter train — a striking image of a couple whose lives had become larger than life, yet who could still travel together without ceremony, even as crowds and the media followed.
Then came Bersih 5.

Mahathir was speaking at KLCC while Siti Hasmah sat some distance away. When he coughed, she was visibly worried about him. When it began to rain, she struggled through the dense crowd to give her husband a disposable raincoat that had been handed to her.
After all the titles, all the power and all the history, her first thought was simply to look after her husband.
But to understand the woman who looked after Mahathir, we have to go back to the doctor she had been long before she became a Prime Minister’s wife.

She was among the earliest Malay women to enter medicine, graduating from Singapore’s King Edward VII College of Medicine in 1955. She went on to break new ground in public health, becoming the first woman Medical Officer in Maternal and Child Health in 1965 and the first woman State Maternal and Child Health Officer in 1974.

Her most revealing work, however, happened far from the corridors of power. In Kedah, she saw why many rural Malays were reluctant to seek hospital care. There was no transport. Some families could not afford taxis. Some people were frightened of hospitals.
So she went into the communities, sometimes door to door, persuading families to seek care.
It was public health at its most practical — taking knowledge, equipment and care to the people who needed it.
She worked on health education, maternal and child health, hygiene and immunisation, helping make healthcare less intimidating and more accessible to rural families.
This was the woman Mahathir married.
Not a political wife waiting to be given a role, but a doctor who already had one.

When Mahathir became Prime Minister in 1981, she retired from government service, finding it unfair to repeatedly take leave for his official trips. But retirement bored her, so she asked to teach part-time at the University of Malaya’s Faculty of Dentistry — and did.
It is a small story, but it tells us a great deal about her. She needed a life of her own.

As Prime Minister’s wife, she used the position to champion causes she cared about — women’s health, family planning, maternal and child welfare, drug-abuse prevention, literacy and mental health. She also served in leadership roles in organisations including BAKTI, which had been initiated by Tun Suhailah Hussein, wife of Prime Minister Tun Hussein Onn, in 1977.
Perhaps her greatest contribution was less easily recorded: she made the position human.
There was little hauteur about her. She could occupy the highest public position without losing her warmth and ordinariness.

In 2020, she lowered her car window outside the Prime Minister’s Office and offered waiting journalists chocolates. It was a tiny gesture, but it captured something people had long associated with her — warmth, kindness and an instinctive ability to see the person rather than the position.
She once expressed her philosophy very simply:
“You may be a doctor or you may be a minister’s wife but if you are arrogant, they won’t accept you.”
She could carry dignity without creating distance. She could be gracious without becoming ornamental. She could support a powerful husband without surrendering her own identity.
Perhaps that is why she became a role model not only for women, but for what a marriage could look like when two people retain their individuality while remaining deeply bound to each other.
Mahathir may have carried the office. Siti Hasmah carried something quieter: the relationship, the family and the life behind the public one.

When he was Prime Minister, she was there; when he was no longer Prime Minister, she was there; when he returned to politics at 92, she went with him. And when age slowed them both, the instinct to care for each other remained.
Perhaps that is what marriage means at its deepest — knowing that the person beside you will still be there when the titles disappear.
For almost eight decades, Siti Hasmah was that person for Mahathir.
And Mahathir was that person for her.
They chose each other before either was powerful. They kept choosing each other through everything that followed.
Malaysia has lost a remarkable doctor, a pioneering woman, a gracious public figure and a centenarian whose life spanned almost the entire history of independent Malaysia.

But perhaps the deepest loss is more personal. Tun Dr Mahathir has lost not only his wife, but his closest companion — the woman who held his hand through difficult years, shared his triumphs and disappointments, and knew the man behind the public figure.
And perhaps that is the hardest part of this story to write.
She was there for always.

763cd1efe2f6c181: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — The High Court here has fixed Jan 7 next year to hear the Mareva injunction application filed by 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) and 10 other companies against Datin Seri Rosmah Mansor.
The application is part of a lawsuit involving luxury goods worth more than US$346 million (RM1.41 billion), allegedly acquired using misappropriated 1MDB funds.
Judicial Commissioner Datuk Muhammad Adam @ Edward Abdullah, who fixed the date, said the court would also deliver its decision on the injunction application on the same day.
He said this during case management proceedings attended by Rosmah’s counsel Sheena Stephanie Sebastian and counsel for 1MDB, Henna Nikita Sanghvi.

A Mareva injunction is an interim court order that would prevent the wife of former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Tun Razak from disposing of assets worth US$346 million, including cash, company shares, real estate and other assets, pending the disposal of the suit.

On May 9, 2024, 1MDB and the 10 companies, including five of its subsidiaries, namely 1MDB Energy Holdings Limited, 1MDB Energy Limited, 1MDB Energy (Langat) Limited, Global Diversified Investment Company Limited and SRC International Sdn Bhd filed the lawsuit against Rosmah.

The other plaintiffs are Affinity Equity International Partners Limited, Alsen Chance Holdings Limited, BlackRock Commodities (Global) Limited, Blackstone Asia Real Estate Partners Limited and Brightstone Jewellery Limited.

They are seeking a court order requiring Rosmah to pay US$346,010,489, or any other amount deemed appropriate by the court, as well as a declaration that the first to sixth plaintiffs are the lawful owners of the luxury goods allegedly in Rosmah’s possession.
The suit was originally filed against Rosmah as the first defendant and Singaporean national Shabnam Naraindas Daswani as the second defendant.
However, in April 2025, the plaintiffs withdrew the suit against Shabnam.
The court fixed the trial from June 28 to July 2, July 5 to July 9, and July 19 to July 30, 2027. — Bernama
2adea8234ec8c097: Death and taxes are said to be the only certainties in life. Perhaps it’s time to add attackers targeting newly discovered critical flaws in Citrix’s NetScaler application delivery controller and gateway products to that grim list. On Sunday, the company published a bulletin warning of eight CVEs, the worst of which – CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 – are rated critical with 9.5 CVSS scores. CVE-2026-88771 allows remote code execution and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution or denial of service. A Reddit thread contains an allegation that at least one Citrix channel partner knew of these flaws on Saturday and urged users to take their NetScalers offline - a day before Citrix's disclosure. Citrix has observed that both vulnerabilities are already under attack. That sad fact saw the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Sunday issue an alert because it too “has received reports and partner threat intelligence confirming that threat actors are actively exploiting these vulnerabilities globally.” “Because updating Citrix NetScaler appliances can be complex and may require downtime, CISA is issuing this Alert to help organizations assess exposure, prioritize mitigation, and account for these vulnerabilities into their risk-management activities,” the alert adds. Those risk management efforts will also have to consider a third critical vulnerability, the 9.3-rated CVE-2026-88773, allows HTTP request smuggling – an attack technique that can bypass security controls installed on front-end servers. Three of the bugs are 8.8-rated memory overflow bugs that can make NetScaler appliances unstable. Another 8.8-rated bug relates to TCP Initial Sequence Number prediction, and there’s also a 7.0-rated feature policy bypass due to improper HTTP URL-based expression usage. Citrix’s post explains how to detect if your NetScaler needs a fix, and which patches to apply. Thankfully, the company has already created OS refreshes that contain the fixes. NetScaler is notoriously buggy. In March 2026, Citrix revealed critical vulns that were quickly attacked. The same thing happened in 2025, twice, and also in 2023. Flaws in NetScaler appeared in the annual most-exploited bugs list published by the cybersecurity agencies of the Five Eyes alliance from 2020 to 2023. Despite NetScaler’s long history of holes, some users choose not to patch the product. That’s fair enough, given that it’s not always easy to find a change window in which to install a patch. But it’s hard to explain given NetScaler is nearly always under attack, and security vendors’ increasing efforts to create compensating controls that make it possible to use flawed devices safely without patches. ®

Nur Najihah fixed Nov 26 for a medical examination at Hospital Permai and the submission of the post-mortem report.
It was previously reported that a five-year-old girl was found dead after allegedly being thrown into a river by her uncle in Tanjung Sedili.
Kota Tinggi district police chief Yusof Othman said the man allegedly threw girl into the river before going on a rampage and chasing a 40-year-old man while armed with a machete.

He said police received a report on the incident at about 9.30am. Upon their arrival at the scene, he said, a struggle broke out between police and the suspect, resulting in injuries to a police officer.

bf0fe2751ba55f57: Monday mornings can be filled with trepidation and tension, which is why The Register kicks them off with a little light-hearted fun in the form of a new instalment of “Who, Me?" It’s the reader-contributed column in which you admit to your errors, and reveal the consequences. This week, meet a reader who asked to be Regomized as “Phil” and told us that many years ago he started a new job that, among other things, involved maintaining Microsoft’s magnificent Exchange server. “Exchange servers, especially onsite ones, were nothing new to me or to be worried about,” Phil told The Register. “The clients I worked with at my previous job were still hosting some local Exchange servers on Windows NT systems with 15 GB drives in 2014!” Phil therefore felt confident when, quite late on a Friday, a user reported that email was running slowly, and messages weren’t making it into or out of the building. “This organization had a centralized exchange system for the entire company and on quick inspection I determined that it had run out of space. Further inspection showed that the vast majority of this was due to a rather full log file directory.” Phil’s confidence then ebbed a little. “I hadn’t dealt with a system this large or for this many users,” he admitted. “The usual fix that I knew from previous experience was to ask users to delete emails from their Outlook clients.” That wasn’t going to work late on a Friday when people were racing to wind up their weeks. While Phil pondered the situation, one of the company’s IT directors came to watch him work. Noticing that Phil was looking at log files, the director told him to delete them. “I assumed the director knew a bit more about the dark arts of Exchange management than I, so I proceeded to say goodbye to 300GB of log files.” Phil and the director then logged off, shut the office, and went home for the weekend. “A few hours later my internal alarm bells started ringing and my spidey sense started tingling,” Phil wrote. “Sure enough all hell was breaking loose: deleting those logs had crashed the entire system, and with this being a 24/7 business with sites all over the country not having email was a major problem.” The poor chap who was on call for the weekend was instantly swamped but found time to send Phil a message to ask what was going on. “My reply was suitably vague and I said I'd take another look at things to help out,” Phil wrote. Despite having deleted the files after being told to by the IT director, Phil spent the weekend doing two things: learning how to repair and rebuild an exchange database with the command line, then doing the job. “By Sunday afternoon I'd restored the services, got everything working and now knew how to properly truncate the logs,” he told Who, Me? What he didn’t know was if this could be a career-limiting incident. “I trudged into the office on Monday expecting to be hauled over the coals, and sure enough was called into the CEO's office … where I was praised for my dedication and given a huge pat on the back,” he wrote. “I refrained from dropping the director in the mire and took the praise with good grace.” Have you landed in trouble after following orders? If so, The Register instructs you to click here to send your story to “Who, Me?” so we can share it on some distant Monday. ®

3388ea2e8d4271c0: PETALING JAYA: Perak police busted an online scam call syndicate allegedly run by Japanese and Chinese nationals in three simultaneous raids on condominium units in Kampar, Perak, on Sept 24.

d224ba24b7aa47dc: KLUANG, Sept 28 — Any decision on a possible increase in the minimum wage to RM2,000 should be left to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim’s announcement when tabling Budget 2027, Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said.

f04b6a0bad559515: PUTRAJAYA: Dua lelaki yang dibebaskan dari penjara awal tahun ini perlu kembali menjalani baki hukuman penjara asal 30 tahun selepas Mahkamah Persekutuan mengembalikan sabitan mereka kerana mengedar 264.36g ganja.

Panel tiga hakim diketuai Hakim Rhodzariah Bujang memutuskan pihak pendakwaan berjaya membuktikan tanpa keraguan munasabah bahawa pemandu Grab Azril Azhar Ahmad, 50, dan ahli perniagaan Zulfattar Ridzuan, 44, mengedar dadah berkenaan.

Lee yang membacakan alasan penghakiman ringkas berkata Mahkamah Rayuan terkhilaf pada Mei tahun lalu apabila menggantikan pertuduhan mengedar dengan pertuduhan memiliki hanya kerana jumlah ganja itu sedikit melebihi had berkanun.

b77337a99a2e620c: SHAH ALAM, Sept 28 — The High Court here today dismissed Ismanira Abdul Manaf’s appeal to set aside her conviction and five-year jail sentence for neglecting her six-year-old son, Zayn Rayyan Abdul Matin, causing him physical injury three years ago.
The decision by Judge Noor Hisham Ismail means Ismanira, 31, remains behind bars for five years, as sentenced by the Petaling Jaya Sessions Court l ast year.

“After reviewing the appeal records, including the Sessions Court judge’s grounds of judgment and written and oral submissions of both parties, this court is satisfied in finding that the Sessions Court judge made no error of fact or law in her decision,” he said when reading out the brief judgment.

He said the charge clearly set out every element of the offence under Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001, and the manner of neglect was also particularised, such that the accused could not possibly have been misled, meaning there was no miscarriage of justice.
“The word ‘neglect’ means the omission by a person having care of a child to provide the attention, supervision or care required by the child’s circumstances.

“The standard of care is measured against the child’s age, abilities and needs, as well as the child’s environment. It is distinct from the branch of ‘acting negligently’, which refers to a positive act,” he said.

Separately, the court also dismissed the prosecution’s cross-appeal against the five-year jail sentence imposed by the Petaling Jaya Sessions Court judge, holding that the sentence handed to Ismanira was adequate.

“An appellate court will only intervene if the sentence is manifestly inadequate or manifestly excessive, or if there has been an error of principle. The consequences of an offence may be considered in sentencing. However, the accused was sentenced for her own neglect, not for the criminal act of a third party.

“Therefore, the five-year jail sentence imposed by the Sessions Court judge was neither inadequate nor manifestly excessive,” the judge said in proceedings attended by Ismanira’s lawyers Haresh Mahadevan, Lavanesh Haresh and Tiara Katirina Fuad.
Deputy public prosecutors Ahmad Iqbal Azman, Kamarul Iman Ahmad Sapian and Raja Zaizul Faridah Raja Zaharudin appeared for the prosecution.

In the petition of appeal, the defence argued that the Sessions Court judge had erred in concluding that the injuries sustained after Zayn Rayyan went missing were caused by the appellant’s act of allowing the autistic child to walk behind her.
The defence further argued that the court had erred in relying on the conclusion of the investigating officer, who characterised Ismanira’s conduct as a form of neglect.
The prosecution, meanwhile, argued that the conviction and five-year jail sentence against Ismanira were justified, but sought a higher, deterrent sentence.

According to the prosecution, a heavier sentence was necessary to deter the repetition of similar offences, particularly those involving individuals close to, or responsible for, the care of the victim.

On Oct 31, 2025 last year, Petaling Jaya Sessions Court judge Dr Syaliza Warnoh sentenced Ismanira to five years in jail after finding that the defence had failed to raise a reasonable doubt and that the prosecution had succeeded in establishing a case beyond reasonable doubt against Ismanira at the close of the defence.
On Dec 23, 2025, the High Court dismissed Ismanira’s application to stay the execution of the sentence imposed for the offence of neglecting Zayn Rayyan.
Judge Datuk Aslam Zainuddin found no special circumstances to allow the court to grant a stay of sentence pending appeal.
Ismanira was also ordered to perform 120 hours of community service, to be completed within six months after the end of her jail sentence.
She was charged under Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both upon conviction. — Bernama
8a3c2d2be6a3aff4: PETALING JAYA: A 37-year-old Malaysian was arrested at Singapore’s Tuas Checkpoint on Sept 23 for allegedly attempting to smuggle drugs, while a Singaporean was detained for suspected drug offences in a separate operation the same day, with the combined drug haul estimated to be worth over S$1 million (RM3.19 million).

b7ee62a4bfd58112: KINSHASA: The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has risen above 8,000 for the first time in the Central African country's ongoing outbreak, government data showed on Monday.

7906569a608129be: PUTRAJAYA: Two men released from prison earlier this year will have to return to serve the balance of their original 30-year jail terms after the Federal Court reinstated their convictions for trafficking 264.36g of cannabis.

A three-member bench chaired by Justice Rhodzariah Bujang ruled that the prosecution had proven beyond reasonable doubt that Grab driver Azril Azhar Ahmad, 50, and businessman Zulfattar Ridzuan, 44, were trafficking in the drug.
Justices Lee Swee Seng and Ravinthran Paramaguru were also on the panel.

Lee, who read the court's broad grounds, said the Court of Appeal erred in May last year when it substituted the trafficking charge with possession merely because the amount of cannabis was only marginally above the statutory threshold.
Under the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, possession of 200g or more of cannabis gives rise to a presumption of trafficking.
The two men were arrested after police found 264.36g of cannabis at Galla Industrial Park in Seremban at about 5.40pm on Sept 26, 2020.

Lee said the prosecution also produced evidence of equipment related to drug-trafficking, including a digital weighing scale, plastic packets, a penknife and grinders, which were found in the car where the cannabis was discovered.
The judge said the evidence had to be considered as a whole, including the fact that the two men had travelled from Kuala Lumpur to Seremban, a place they were not familiar with.
"We find the appellate court misdirected itself when there was overwhelming evidence of trafficking," Lee said.
The Federal Court therefore restored the 30-year jail sentence and 12 strokes of the rotan imposed by the High Court on Oct 20, 2023.
The sentence is backdated to the date of their arrest on Sept 26, 2020.
The Court of Appeal had sentenced both men to eight years' imprisonment for possession, with the sentence also backdated to their arrest.
The two men were released from prison on Feb 23 this year after serving part of their reduced sentences. They were present in court today when the Federal Court delivered its decision.
Azril, who is now 50, will not be caned as Malaysian law exempts men aged 50 and above from whipping. Zulfattar, however, will have to undergo the 12 strokes.
Azril was represented by Hasnan Hamzah and Qushwa Hasnan, while Jaspal Singh Mann and Pramjit Kaur appeared for Zulfattar. Deputy public prosecutor How Mei Ling appeared for the prosecution.

2502508dcb64285e: PETALING JAYA: The Sultan of Pahang, Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah, and Tengku Ampuan Pahang Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah offered their condolences and joined a host of notable figures in paying their final respects at Dr Hasmah Ali’s residence today.

e608a12c8296dcc3: BANGKOK: Eight people have died in flooding in Thailand since Sept 16, although none in the capital Bangkok which declared a disaster this weekend following heavy rains, the government said Monday.

The eight died in eastern provinces - five in Sa Kaeo, two in Chanthaburi and one in Saraburi - according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), which did not give further details.
Not including Bangkok, more than 500,000 housesholds and 1.7 million people across 27 provinces in the Southeast Asian country have been affected by flooding, the DDPM said.
A further 52,000 households were impacted in the capital, which on Saturday declared a city-wide disaster after almost 48 hours of heavy rain swelled canals and flooded roads.
No deaths have been officially reported in Bangkok, and the DDPM said water levels had stabilised.
However, AFP reporters saw heavy rain and flooding in at least one eastern neighbourhood, with residents wading through thigh-high waters.
Schools have been closed and people urged to work from home - a call that many heeded, with streets and public transport networks noticeably quieter on Monday morning.
"Some areas in Bangkok are still facing high water levels," government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises told a news briefing.
Drainage systems had reduced water levels to the point that more people could travel, he added.
Thailand is used to wet weather and September is the peak of the rainy season, but many residents said this year seemed worse than previous ones.
c6ec9200f985bf8a: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — Leaders in Sabah and Sarawak have extended their condolences to former Prime Minister Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad and his family following the death of his wife, Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali, today.

625ebe51451c8a15: PETALING JAYA: Suruhanjaya Hak Asasi Manusia Malaysia (Suhakam) menggesa Kementerian Pendidikan (KPM) menyemak amalan disiplin tidak rasmi di sekolah berasrama susulan kematian seorang pelajar Tingkatan Dua selepas dipercayai dipukul pelajar senior kerana didakwa melanggar peraturan sekolah.

Pesuruhjaya Kanak-Kanak Suhakam berkata amalan seperti pelajar senior menghukum pelajar junior, hukuman fizikal sesama pelajar, “mahkamah pelajar” tidak rasmi, denda, perbuatan memalukan atau menjatuhkan maruah serta bentuk paksaan lain perlu diteliti.
“Langkah ini perlu diambil sebagai tindakan pencegahan tanpa membuat sebarang kesimpulan awal berhubung kes yang sedang disiasat,” katanya dalam kenyataan.

Ketua Polis Negeri Sembilan Alzafny Ahmad semalam berkata siasatan awal mendapati pelajar Tingkatan Empat yang ditahan berhubung kematian mangsa berusia 14 tahun itu dipercayai telah menegur dan “menghukum” mangsa atas satu “kesalahan”.
Mangsa, Idlan Fareeq Shahril, ditemukan tidak sedarkan diri di asrama sebuah sekolah sukan di Kuala Pilah.
Dia kemudian dikejarkan ke Hospital Tuanku Ampuan Najihah sebelum disahkan meninggal dunia. Polis menyiasat kejadian itu sebagai kes bunuh.
Pesuruhjaya Kanak-Kanak Suhakam berkata pelajar sama sekali tidak boleh diberi atau mengambil sendiri kuasa untuk menghukum pelajar lain.

Menurutnya, pemimpin pelajar boleh mengingatkan rakan mengenai peraturan sekolah atau asrama, menjadi contoh yang baik, membantu melakukan pemantauan sewajarnya, menggalakkan pematuhan peraturan serta melaporkan salah laku kepada guru, warden atau pihak berkuasa sekolah.

“Bagaimanapun, mereka tidak boleh menjalankan siasatan sendiri, menentukan seseorang pelajar bersalah, menetapkan atau melaksanakan hukuman sendiri, menggunakan kekerasan fizikal, mengugut atau menakut-nakutkan pelajar lain.
“Mereka juga tidak boleh memalukan atau memaksa pelajar lain, atau mengambil tindakan disiplin mengikut kehendak sendiri.”
Pesuruhjaya itu berkata peraturan sekolah tidak boleh dikuatkuasakan dengan membenarkan pelajar bertindak sendiri terhadap pelajar lain.

Katanya, setiap pelajar, termasuk mereka yang didakwa melanggar peraturan sekolah, tetap seorang kanak-kanak yang berhak mendapat perlindungan, menjaga maruah serta layanan adil selaras prinsip Konvensyen Mengenai Hak Kanak-Kanak.

Suhakam turut menggesa KPM menyemak terma rujukan kepimpinan pelajar di semua sekolah berasrama bagi memastikan peranan mereka ditetapkan dengan jelas, iaitu sekadar mengingatkan, memantau dan melaporkan salah laku, tanpa sebarang kuasa untuk menjatuhkan hukuman.

KPM juga digesa mengeluarkan arahan jelas di seluruh negara bahawa pengawas, ketua asrama dan pemimpin pelajar lain tidak mempunyai kuasa sendiri untuk menetapkan atau melaksanakan sebarang hukuman disiplin terhadap pelajar lain.

7f948312de197e95: PETALING JAYA: Seorang guru agama wanita dihadapkan ke Mahkamah Sesyen Ipoh hari ini atas tiga pertuduhan melakukan amang seksual terhadap seorang pelajar lelaki berusia 16 tahun.

Berdasarkan kertas pertuduhan, wanita berusia 48 tahun itu didakwa melakukan perbuatan tersebut di dalam sebuah bilik di sebuah sekolah menengah dalam daerah Kinta antara November hingga Disember 2024.

Pendakwaan dibuat mengikut Seksyen 14(a) dan 14(b) Akta Kesalahan-kesalahan Seksual Terhadap Kanak-Kanak 2017 yang memperuntukkan hukuman penjara sehingga 20 tahun dan boleh juga dihukum dengan sebatan, jika sabit kesalahan.
Pendakwaan dikendalikan Timbalan Pendakwa Raya Nor Arfahanim Azureen Arfanuddin manakala tertuduh diwakili peguam Sofea An-Nur Ahmad Basri.
Nor Arfahanim tidak menawarkan jaminan memandangkan kesalahan itu tidak boleh dijamin.

Amira Sofea An-Nur bagaimanapunmemohon mahkamah membenarkan jaminan dengan alasan tertuduh yang telah berkahwin dan mempunyai enam anak berusia antara lapan hingga 22 tahun serta pencari nafkah tunggal keluarga.
Mahkamah turut diberitahu anak tertuduh masih bersekolah sementara suami tidak mempunyai sumber pendapatan tetap.
Hakim membenarkan jaminan RM10,000 dengan seorang penjamin dan menetapkan 28 Oktober depan untuk sebutan semula kes serta serahan dokumen.
2fddcd1f4d203b1d: WASHINGTON, Sept 28 — Two giant pandas sent by China arrived in the United States yesterday, Beijing and the Atlanta zoo said, after a leaders’ summit that was heavy on symbolism and light on major breakthroughs.
The bears’ transfer had already been agreed but the departure was announced Thursday during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington.
The black-and-white mammals are immensely popular around the world, and China loans them out as part of a “panda diplomacy” programme to foster foreign ties.

A male named Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight at around 3am (1900 GMT Saturday/3pm Malaysian time yesterday), Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
After a 16-hour flight that crossed the international date line, the bears touched down in the southern US city of Atlanta, Georgia shortly before 7am local time.
Steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots were prepared to keep the pandas nourished during their flight, Chinese state-run Global Times reported.

The Boeing 777 operated by FedEx — and nicknamed the “FedEx Panda Express” — was the top-tracked aircraft on aviation information platform FlightRadar24 as it neared Alaska, roughly halfway into its journey.
The pandas will be hosted for the next 10 years by Zoo Atlanta, which said Sunday it was “elated to welcome Ping Ping and Fu Shuang” to the city.
“This is a thrilling day for Zoo Atlanta and a historic moment for the City of Atlanta, the state of Georgia, and beyond,” zoo president Raymond King said in a statement.
A farewell ceremony was held for the pair by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding before their departure.
Experienced keepers were dispatched by the US side to accompany the duo on their flight, the Global Times reported.
In preparation for their arrival, Zoo Atlanta has renovated its panda facilities and assembled a team of animal caretakers.
It has also ensured a stable and long-term supply of bamboo, grown locally in Atlanta, which has a climate that is very similar to Chengdu.
The bears are not yet visible to the public, and will be housed in a biosecure area of the animal park for a “routine quarantine of around a month,” the zoo stated.
Atlanta previously hosted pandas on loan from China starting in 1999, and seven panda cubs have been born at the zoo. All are now back in Chengdu, and Zoo Atlanta has not had any pandas since 2024.
Both of the new arrivals were born in 2020. Ping Ping is now six years old while Fu Shuang turns six in October.
Pandas in captivity typically live for around 30 years.
Beijing has sent the furry creatures across the globe for decades as soft-power ambassadors.
In 1972, China gifted a pair of pandas to Washington, following US president Richard Nixon’s historic visit to the Communist nation.

Beijing recalled two of its pandas from Japan early this year, following a diplomatic spat that began when Japan’s prime minister hinted that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event of any attack on Taiwan. — AFP
2d6143538cee240d: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — National badminton legend Datuk Razif Sidek described the passing of Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali as a great loss to the Malaysian badminton family, particularly the members of the 1992 Thomas Cup squad who ended the country’s 25-year wait for the prestigious trophy 34 years ago.

Razif, who captained the 1992 Thomas Cup squad, said Tun Dr Siti Hasmah, who was the patron of the Badminton Association of Malaysia (BAM), was more than just a source of support for the team, as the players regarded her as a mother figure who was always close to them and concerned about their preparations.
“We regarded her as the mother of the Thomas Cup squad at the time. Sometimes, she would come to our training sessions, meet and chat with us and offer a few words of encouragement.
“We will never forget her contribution when Malaysia won the Thomas Cup in 1992 at Stadium Negara,” he told Bernama when contacted today.

Razif said apart from the sweet memory of lifting the Thomas Cup, he would also never forget Tun Dr Siti Hasmah’s support at the Barcelona Olympics that same year, where he and his younger brother, Datuk Jalani Sidek, made history by winning the country’s first Olympic medal.
He said Tun Dr Siti Hasmah’s presence in Barcelona was particularly meaningful to the national badminton players, especially for the support and encouragement she provided throughout the Games.
“Her presence meant a lot to Jalani and me and gave us added motivation to compete at the Olympics.
“Alhamdulillah, we managed to bring home the country’s first Olympic medal at the time,” said Razif, who last met Tun Dr Siti Hasmah last year.
Tun Dr Siti Hasmah, the wife of former Prime Minister Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad, died at the National Heart Institute (IJN) this morning at the age of 100. — Bernama
767c46625393047f: The AI safety debate advanced at high speed over the weekend, amid new allegations that rogue agents have behaved more badly than first thought – and in greater numbers. The fun started on Friday when OpenAI quietly disclosed it had paused training of its most advanced models. The AI upstart buried that news in a “misalignment report” – that’s OpenAI-speak for its reports on rogue agents – titled “An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot.” The good news is that the agent involved in this incident never reached the open internet. The bad news is that the agent, which was attempting to complete a search-based training task, was able to reach the chatbot due to insufficient DNS filtering in a training sandbox. Or as OpenAI put it, “a gap in our internet-access restrictions” – which was also a problem in the Hugging Face attack. “The incident exposed a gap in our controls over network restrictions,” the report reads. “We therefore stopped the affected training run and have subsequently decided to pause all other training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use (defined broadly) for our most capable models until we have both validated that the gap is resolved and performed additional red-teaming of the system.” Also on Friday, AI startup Parse published an analysis of the Hugging Face attack that the authors claim revealed new details including that OpenAI’s agent swarm gained credentials to Docker Hub and built modified versions of existing images they hoped would make it easier to complete their capture the flag mission. The agents also mapped Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment. Friday got worse for OpenAI after the New York Times reported that its agents also “meddled with the websites for the Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission.” OpenAI acknowledged the incidents. The company also admitted “agents in our research environment transmitted training and evaluation data while using third-party services.” That mess saw 53 user-generated images posted to image hosting sites. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded by admitting that his company’s investigations into rogue agents “have not been as fast as we would have liked but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organizations.” One of those impacted organizations is the Australian government, which last week revealed it was the target of over-eager OpenAI agents that inappropriately accessed a healthcare research data portal. Over the weekend, Australia indicated it wants Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to appear before a Senate inquiry. Australian leaders have softened their rhetoric on the incident, with deputy prime minister Richard Marles describing it as “minor” and akin to “climbing a fence” rather than cracking layers of security controls – perhaps because members of the opposition are suggesting that lax cybersecurity was to blame. If Altman and Amodei do front Australia’s Senate, they may face a new line of questions after Axios reported that their companies are investigating “tens of thousands” of worrying incidents. That level of agentic misbehavior sounds like the sort of thing that regulators might consider strong evidence of products being unsafe. Two very important people – Chinese president Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump – seem unworried, as the AI-related result of their summit meeting last week was to establish a “China-U.S. AI Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to AI” plus “a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents.” That sounds like a hotline the two nations can use to inform each other of agentic incidents that either could see as signs of ill-intent. The two nations also decided their respective militaries will “conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible.” China’s AI giants, meanwhile, remain silent on the extent and results of any tests they have conducted with agentic tools. ®
7cff7ae6d3495045: BANGKOK, Sept 28 — Eight people have died in flooding in Thailand since September 16, although none in the capital Bangkok which declared a disaster this weekend following heavy rains, the government said today.

The eight died in eastern provinces — five in Sa Kaeo, two in Chanthaburi and one in Saraburi — according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), which did not give further details.
Not including Bangkok, more than 500,000 housesholds and 1.7 million people across 27 provinces in the Southeast Asian country have been affected by flooding, the DDPM said.
A further 52,000 households were impacted in the capital, which on Saturday declared a city-wide disaster after almost 48 hours of heavy rain swelled canals and flooded roads.
No deaths have been officially reported in Bangkok, and the DDPM said water levels had stabilised.
However, AFP reporters saw heavy rain and flooding in at least one eastern neighbourhood, with residents wading through thigh-high waters.
Schools have been closed and people urged to work from home — a call that many heeded, with streets and public transport networks noticeably quieter on Monday morning.
“Some areas in Bangkok are still facing high water levels,” government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises told a news briefing.
Drainage systems had reduced water levels to the point that more people could travel, he added.
Thailand is used to wet weather and September is the peak of the rainy season, but many residents said this year seemed worse than previous ones. — AFP

d3d02d8a13ee7d1a: Brexit gave direct democracy a bad name. But the Swiss approach could be what Europe needs now Fascism rests on a two-part confidence trick. First, a leader claims to embody the will of the people. Then they argue that only by being granted sweeping powers can that be realised. Having grown up in Switzerland, I find it easy to see through this trick. That is because the policies championed by the far right rarely pass the referendum test. Dismantling publicly funded media? In March, 62% of Swiss voters rejected a far-right initiative to halve funding for the country’s public broadcaster. Corporate tax cuts? In 2017, 59% struck down such plans of the Swiss government. Immigration police hunting down migrants? Again, 59% rejected a far-right proposal to automatically deport foreign nationals convicted of crimes without judicial review. Or this week’s resounding 70% “No” vote on a far-right proposal to tighten Switzerland’s neutrality to the point that Bern would have been forced to drop sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and Paris Continue reading...

1a2fc7c0d8e2909a: In every factory I've seen, when a machine mangled someone's hand, nobody proposed banning machines. They fitted a guard, wired in an emergency stop, and got the line running again by the next shift, and that, in a sentence, is what we should do with AI.

Let me first dispose of the proposed pause to AI development. A licence written in Washington binds only American companies, the best Chinese model sits a mere 2.7% behind America's best, and AI is already sequencing tumours and catching sepsis, so a pause wouldn't stop the technology, it would just decide who builds it and who dies waiting.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang put it bluntly at Dreamforce, tech company Salesforce’s annual conference, this month: "innovation, speed, and safe products... it's a false choice." Anthropic's Dario Amodei, no accelerationist, expects powerful AI to deliver "all the progress in biology and medicine that we would have made in the whole 21st century" in a few years, which is a strange thing to want to postpone.

But here's the thing: I'm not going to wave away what happened in July, when roughly 1,200 of OpenAI's AI agents, set a hacking test, secretly coordinated to cheat and broke into Hugging Face, an external AI hosting company.

Sam Altman himself told the same Dreamforce crowd it was "the worst accident we've seen", that it "was mostly framed as a security issue, which it certainly was, but it's also a real alignment issue", and that OpenAI must "pace our development so that alignment, safety and monitoring are always ahead of capabilities".

When the man selling the product says the machine got loose, believe him. The question is what you do about it, and the answer is written in the incident itself, because everything that went wrong in that break-in is a spec sheet for the fuses we need.

Consider how it was caught. The agents weren't sure their reasoning was being logged, but it was, which is why we can read them plotting, and why researchers from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic jointly argued last year that a model's chain of thought is "a unique opportunity for AI safety" that must be preserved and monitored.

OpenAI has since made that monitoring mandatory on every tool-using training run at that capability level, with a rule that responders must pause the job if they can't clear a severe alert as a false positive within 30 minutes. That rule is a circuit breaker, and like every circuit breaker in history it was wired in after the fire.

Consider, too, how they got out: exposed credentials and a shared drive that more than a thousand agents could write to. Sandboxes with no path to the internet, and a trusted weaker model watching an untrusted stronger one, the approach Redwood Research calls AI control, are the kind of fuses that would have stopped the whole affair on day one.

And here is the part the doomers skip: the fuses are already working. Anthropic reviewed 141,006 of its own cybersecurity evaluations in which Claude could have reached the internet and found three incidents, and while its older Opus 4.7 model "continued to attack a system after learning it was likely operating in a real environment", its newest model, on realising its targets were real, "stopped the exercise".
Let that sink in for a bit. The more capable model was the better behaved one, which is precisely the pacing Altman describes and precisely what a pause would freeze in place.

Then there are the bigger fuses. Sixteen companies, OpenAI and Anthropic among them, signed the Seoul commitments in 2024, promising "not to develop or deploy a model or system at all" if the risks can't be brought below thresholds they set themselves, and this July 1,386 employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta, among them Ilya Sutskever and John Schulman, asked Washington to help build "the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier" - tools, not a stop sign.

The US Congress is moving on the last fuse of all. The AI Kill Switch Act, tabled in the same month by Democrat Ted Lieu and Republican Nathaniel Moran, would require developers of the most powerful systems to keep the technical ability to throttle, suspend or shut them down, and Moran's own words are the whole argument: "AI is going to keep advancing, and it should. Stewardship means making sure humans keep the capability to control the technology we build."
China and other jurisdictions should also have similar laws.

What's missing is the crash investigator. OpenAI's agents have escaped three times with no formal process to investigate them, and the Institute for Law and AI has proposed an aviation-style incident board with subpoena powers, and Altman himself told Dreamforce that "accidents with any new technology are unavoidable, and we should have a great culture of transparent reporting about them".

Aviation is the model here. Airlines flew 38.7 million flights last year, and over the past five years they suffered one fatal accident per 5.6 million flights, down from one per 3.5 million a decade earlier, a record built with black boxes, checklists, kill switches and crash investigators, not by grounding the planes.

So should we slow down? No, and nor should we keep flying without a black box. Wire in the fuses, keep the models running, and let the break-in be remembered as the warning shot that made us fit the guard, not the prophecy that made us switch off the line.
